sermon:
## A Church You Can Read From the Street
*Faith, love, and hope in a congregation the whole province is watching*

**Text:** 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 4:20 · Romans 1:16 · John 5:24 · Titus 2:13

Paul plants a church in Thessalonica, gets run out of town by a mob inside a few weeks, and writes back to a congregation he barely had time to teach. He has every reason to worry about them. He does not. He opens by giving thanks. Not for their programs. Not for their growth strategy. For three things a stranger could see from the outside.

**A gospel that came in power, not in words only**

Paul remembers how the gospel arrived. "Our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance" (1 Thessalonians 1:5). We have built an entire industry on the opposite of that distinction. We have learned to produce the word without the power. We can run the lights, work the room, land the close, and never once depend on the Spirit to do anything we could not engineer ourselves. Paul could not. He came to a hostile city with nothing but a message and the God behind it, and something happened that no rhetorician could manufacture.

This is what he meant when he told the Corinthians, "the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power" (1 Corinthians 4:20). The word is the means. The power is the proof. A church can have flawless words and be dead. Paul says these people had both, and he knew which one he could not take credit for. He even tells them what kind of men he and his companions had to become to bring it: "as ye know what manner of men we were among you for your sake" (1 Thessalonians 1:5). The power came through preachers who let their lives be read alongside their words. The two could not be pried apart.

**Faith that works, love that labors, hope that endures**

Then comes the line the whole letter hangs on. He remembers "your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of God" (1 Thessalonians 1:3). Faith is not idle here; it works. Love is not a feeling here; it labors. Hope is not a mood here; it bears weight under pressure. Three Christian words we have softened into sentiment, and Paul attaches a hard verb to every one of them. The verbs are the point. A faith that never works was never faith. A love that never labors was never love. A hope that collapses the first time it is leaned on was never the hope of the gospel.

And he says he saw it. "Knowing, brethren beloved, your election of God" (1 Thessalonians 1:4). How does a man claim to know another man's election? Not by reading a heart he cannot see. By reading a life he can. The gospel came in power, the power produced faith and love and hope, and the faith and love and hope made a noise the whole region could hear. "From you sounded out the word of the Lord not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith to God-ward is spread abroad" (1 Thessalonians 1:8). They did not run a campaign. They lived in a way that traveled. The verb Paul uses is the sound of a trumpet, their faith blew like a horn across the province, and they were not the ones blowing it. This is the gospel Paul was unashamed of, the one he said "is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth" (Romans 1:16), not a private opinion held quietly, but a power that gets out.

**The reception that cost them something**

There is a detail in here we read past too fast. They "received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Ghost" (1 Thessalonians 1:6). The word came, and the trouble came with it, and they took both at once. That is how Paul knew it was real. A gospel that costs you nothing on the way in is usually a gospel that was never received at all. These people lost something the day they believed, standing, safety, neighbors who used to be friends, and they had joy anyway, the joy that does not come from circumstances and therefore cannot be taken by them. They became, Paul says, "followers of us, and of the Lord," and then "ensamples to all that believe" (1 Thessalonians 1:6-7). The disciples became the pattern. The new church became the model the older churches looked at.

**What they were waiting for**

Here is the part that exposes us. Paul names what their hope was actually fixed on. They had "turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God; and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, even Jesus, which delivered us from the wrath to come" (1 Thessalonians 1:9-10).

To wait for his Son from heaven. That is the engine under the whole church. Not waiting for the economy to turn. Not waiting for the persecution to stop. Waiting for a Person to come down out of heaven, the same Person God raised from the dead, who stands between them and a wrath they had earned and could not escape on their own. Jesus said it plainly: "He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life" (John 5:24). Passed already. The verdict already rendered. And so they could wait without flinching, "looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ" (Titus 2:13).

I have to ask myself what I am actually waiting for, because my anxieties tell on me. I worry like a man whose hope is in the next quarter, not the returning Lord. I plan like a man who expects history to end with me comfortable, not with Christ descending. And when I am honest, my faith does not labor and my love does not cost and my hope does not endure, because somewhere I stopped waiting for his Son and started waiting for an easier life. I have preached patience of hope to a congregation while privately staking my own peace on things that cannot bear the weight. The Thessalonians had nothing. They had a Lord who was coming. It turned out to be everything.

That is why their hope did not need to be advertised. It announced itself. A church that is genuinely waiting for Christ to return cannot be hidden, because the waiting changes how they hold money and grief and danger and time, and a watching city notices people who are not afraid of the things that frighten everyone else. They did not have to tell Macedonia what they believed. Macedonia could read it off their lives.

Their waiting was their witness.

## The Minister Who Has Nothing to Hide
*A ministry that answers to God and not to the crowd*

**Text:** 1 Thessalonians 2:1-12 · **Supporting:** Galatians 1:10 · 2 Corinthians 4:2 · John 10:11 · Acts 20:33-34

Paul has enemies in Thessalonica, and they are doing what enemies of preachers have always done: they are not arguing his doctrine, they are attacking his motives. He came for money. He came for a following. He came to use you. So Paul answers, and watch how he answers. He does not produce a single credential. He recalls how he came.

**He did not come to please you**

"For our exhortation was not of deceit, nor of uncleanness, nor in guile" (1 Thessalonians 2:3). And then the line that should make every man who stands behind a pulpit go quiet: "even so we speak; not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts" (1 Thessalonians 2:4). Not as pleasing men. He had said the same thing to the Galatians and dared them to check his record: "do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Galatians 1:10).

This is the fork every minister stands at, and most of us pretend it is not there. You cannot serve two audiences. The crowd and God want different things from you, and the day you start managing the crowd's approval is the day you stop speaking for God, because the crowd will always pay you to soften exactly the thing God sent you to say. I know this temptation from the inside. I have edited a sermon for the room instead of for the Lord. I have felt the pull to land softer because softer keeps people coming back, and I have called that wisdom when it was cowardice wearing wisdom's coat. Paul refuses the whole transaction. He renounced, as he told the Corinthians, "the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully" (2 Corinthians 4:2). No spin. No managing. The text says what it says.

And he refused the two oldest tools of the religious con man. "Neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness" (1 Thessalonians 2:5). Flattery and greed, the salesman tells you what you want to hear so he can get what he wants from you. Paul did neither. He did not "seek glory of men," he says, though as an apostle he could have thrown his weight around and demanded it (1 Thessalonians 2:6). The man who could have made them serve him chose to serve them. That is the credential, and it is the only one he offers.

**A nursing mother and an exhorting father**

Then Paul does something the cynics never expect. Having said he will not flatter them, he tells them how tenderly he loved them. "We were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children" (1 Thessalonians 2:7). A nursing mother holding her own infant, there is no gentler picture in the ancient world, and Paul reaches for it to describe his own ministry to grown men. And the cost is in the next line: "we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were dear unto us" (1 Thessalonians 2:8).

Not the gospel only. Also our own souls. He did not deliver a message and leave. He handed them the truth and handed them himself, and you cannot fake that, and you cannot do it at scale, and you cannot do it from a stage. You do it the way he did it: "labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable to any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God" (1 Thessalonians 2:9). He worked a job so his preaching would cost them nothing, the same conviction he threw down before the Ephesian elders: "I have coveted no man's silver, or gold... these hands have ministered unto my necessities" (Acts 20:33-34).

And the tenderness had a spine. "We exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father doth his children, that ye would walk worthy of God" (1 Thessalonians 2:11-12). The mother cherishes. The father charges. Both at once, or it is neither. A ministry that only comforts produces children who never grow. A ministry that only charges produces children who never come home. Paul was both because love is both. And note the words "every one of you", not a crowd worked from a distance but persons known one at a time, the slow, unscalable, face-by-face labor that no platform has ever been able to reproduce.

**The Shepherd behind the shepherd**

Now turn it, because Paul is not finally pointing at himself. He is showing them a pattern, and the pattern has an origin. Every true under-shepherd is a copy, and the original said, "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep" (John 10:11). That is the sentence under Paul's whole self-defense. He gave them the gospel and his own soul because the One he served gave the sheep His own blood. The minister who has nothing to hide is only following the Master who hid nothing, who did not flatter the crowd that wanted bread without a cross, who set His face toward Jerusalem and went.

And this is the standard I am measured by, and you with me. We have learned to evaluate ministry by reach. God evaluates it by motive, "God, which trieth our hearts." The question on the last day will not be how many heard you. It will be who you were speaking to please while you spoke. The crowd cannot try your heart; it can only count your numbers. The Lord who is coming back will do the other thing. He will read the motives no congregation could see, and He will not be impressed by a single thing that was done to be seen. The only minister ready for that day is the one with nothing to hide, the one whose private motives could be read aloud in heaven without a single edit, and the same is true of every Christian, because we all serve some audience, and the day is coming when the only One in the room will be the One who tries the heart.

He gave them the gospel and himself.

## When the Report Comes Back
*A separated apostle, a sent messenger, and a faith that stands*

**Text:** 1 Thessalonians 2:17-3:13 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 16:13 · Philippians 1:8 · John 16:33 · 1 Peter 5:10

Paul is in Athens, then Corinth, and he cannot get back to Thessalonica. He says Satan hindered him (1 Thessalonians 2:18), and whatever that means, the effect is plain: he is cut off from a church he loves and cannot reach. And he is not calm about it. We have made the apostle Paul into a granite figure who feels nothing. Read this chapter and watch him come apart.

**Love that cannot sit still**

"We, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire" (1 Thessalonians 2:17). Taken from you. The word behind it is the word for being orphaned, and Paul reaches for it on purpose. Separation from these people feels to him like bereavement. This is the same man who told the Philippians, "I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:8). He does not love his churches at a professional distance. He aches for them. He even calls them his trophy on the last day: "what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Are not even ye in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? For ye are our glory and joy" (1 Thessalonians 2:19-20). When Christ returns, Paul wants nothing in his hands but people. That is the only treasure he is taking to that day.

So he does the costly thing. "When we could no longer forbear, we thought it good to be left at Athens alone; and sent Timotheus" (1 Thessalonians 3:1-2). Read what that sentence costs. To be left at Athens alone. Paul gives up his last companion, accepts isolation in a strange and hostile city, and sends his most trusted man away, because he would rather suffer the loneliness himself than leave the church without help. That is what love does. It absorbs the cost so someone else does not have to.

**Why he sent: that no man be moved**

And he tells them exactly why he sent Timothy: "to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith: that no man should be moved by these afflictions" (1 Thessalonians 3:2-3). He was not checking attendance. He was afraid the persecution would shake them loose. "For this cause, when I could no longer forbear, I sent to know your faith, lest by some means the tempter have tempted you, and our labour be in vain" (1 Thessalonians 3:5).

He is not pretending the afflictions are not real. He told them in advance they were coming: "we told you before that we should suffer tribulation; even as it came to pass" (1 Thessalonians 3:4). This is the faith no one sells you on a stage, the faith that knows tribulation is not a sign something went wrong but the very thing Christ promised. "In the world ye shall have tribulation," Jesus said, "but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). Paul says we are "appointed thereunto" (1 Thessalonians 3:3), affliction is the appointment, not the accident. He wanted them established, the way Christ commanded the whole church: "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong" (1 Corinthians 16:13). Stand fast. Not feel good. Stand.

**The report, and the life it gave him**

Then Timothy comes back. And the whole chapter breaks open. "Now when Timotheus came from you unto us, and brought us good tidings of your faith and charity... we were comforted over you in all our affliction and distress by your faith: for now we live, if ye stand fast in the Lord" (1 Thessalonians 3:6-8).

For now we live. Hear how far gone he was. The man could not breathe until he knew they were standing, and when the report came back that they were, it was resurrection to him. "What thanks can we render to God again for you, for all the joy wherewith we joy for your sakes before our God; night and day praying exceedingly that we might see your face, and might perfect that which is lacking in your faith?" (1 Thessalonians 3:9-10). Their standing was not a line on his ministry report. It was his life.

And now turn it onto us, because we keep ministry at a safer distance than this. We will pray for people. We will not be undone by them. We have learned to care about the church the way you care about a project, invested, but able to sleep. Paul could not sleep. He prayed night and day. He could not be comforted by his own success while they were in danger. And I have to ask whether my calm is maturity or whether it is distance, whether I have grown wise or merely stopped letting people cost me anything. I have stood at a healthy distance from people's faith and called it boundaries when it was simply the refusal to be hurt.

But notice where Paul finally puts the weight. He does not trust their willpower to keep them standing. He prays, "the Lord make you to increase and abound in love... to the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints" (1 Thessalonians 3:12-13). The Lord stablish you. At the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. There it is again, the horizon the whole letter bends toward. Their faith would stand not because they were strong but because the One who is coming back is faithful, "the God of all grace... who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus," who Himself will "stablish, strengthen, settle you" (1 Peter 5:10). Paul sweated over their standing because he loved them. God guaranteed it because He is coming for them. Paul prayed night and day for a thing the returning Christ had already promised to do, and that is not wasted prayer. It is how the promise gets prayed into a frightened church.

Their standing was his life.

## The Will of God You Already Know
*Holiness in the body, love among the brothers, a quiet working life*

**Text:** 1 Thessalonians 4:1-12 · **Supporting:** Hebrews 12:14 · 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 · Romans 12:10 · 1 Peter 1:15-16

People search for the will of God as if it were buried. We treat it like a hidden coordinate, which city, which job, which person, and we wait for a sign that rarely comes. Paul tells a young church what the will of God is, and it is not hidden at all. It is so plain it offends us. "This is the will of God, even your sanctification" (1 Thessalonians 4:3). You want to know God's will for your life. Here it is. Be holy. Now we have to deal with what that actually means, because Paul does not leave it as a slogan. He puts a body on it.

And he frames it as a continuation, not a graduation. "As ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more" (1 Thessalonians 4:1). They were already walking this way. He does not tell them to start; he tells them to abound, to keep going further into a road they were already on. Holiness is never finished. There is no plateau where a Christian has arrived and may now coast.

**Holiness has a body**

He goes straight to the place we least want him to go. "That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour; not in the lust of concupiscence... that no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter" (1 Thessalonians 4:4-6). Control your body. In honor, not in passion. He is talking about sexual purity, and he refuses to be vague about it, in a city where temple prostitution was ordinary worship and using another person's body was simply what bodies were for.

We are not in a different city. We are in the same one with better screens. And the church has largely surrendered here, deciding this is the one area where private freedom outranks the command of God. Paul will not allow it, and his reason is not that the body is dirty. His reason is the opposite. "Know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you... ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price" (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). The body is holy ground because Christ paid for it. To defile it is not a private matter. It is robbing the One who bought it. And Paul warns plainly "that the Lord is the avenger of all such" and adds the line that closes the door on our self-deception: "He therefore that despiseth, despiseth not man, but God, who hath also given unto us his holy Spirit" (1 Thessalonians 4:6, 4:8). Despise the command and you have not disagreed with a preacher. You have despised God, the God who put His own Spirit in the very body you are deciding to dishonor.

I cannot preach this from above it. No man can. The pull toward using the body for pleasure instead of honoring it for God is in me as surely as in anyone hearing this, and the only honest way to preach holiness is from inside the fight, not from some imagined high ground I do not occupy. The man who preaches purity as though he has never felt its opposite is lying, and the people in the pews know it.

**Holiness has a neighbor**

Then Paul widens it. "As touching brotherly love ye need not that I write unto you: for ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another. And indeed ye do it... but we beseech you, brethren, that ye increase more and more" (1 Thessalonians 4:9-10). He does not scold them here. He commends them and then says: more. Holiness is not only what you refuse to do with your body. It is what you actually do with your brother. "Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another" (Romans 12:10). The same heart that honors the body honors the neighbor, because both belong to God. And catch how he describes the source of their love, "taught of God." Nobody handed them a curriculum on it. God Himself wrote love into them when He saved them, and the evidence that a man has been taught of God is not that he can explain love but that he does it, and keeps doing more of it.

**Holiness has a Monday**

And then Paul lands it somewhere no one expects a holiness sermon to go. "Study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands... that ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing" (1 Thessalonians 4:11-12). Holiness shows up at a job. Mind your own affairs. Work with your hands. Do not become a burden, do not become a busybody, earn the respect of the outsiders watching you by being the kind of person who pays his own way and keeps his word on a Tuesday.

This is where we have it backwards. We imagine holiness as the dramatic spiritual experience and the workweek as the place we endure until Sunday. Paul says the holiness is in the workweek. The quiet, faithful, self-supporting life that owes no one and serves everyone is not the absence of the spiritual life. It is the spiritual life, lived where the watching world can see it. And the world is watching, "them that are without." A church that prays loudly on Sunday and cannot be trusted on Monday has already lost the argument with its neighbors, no matter how good the singing was.

And under it all is the same horizon and the same Person. "Be ye holy in all manner of conversation; because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy" (1 Peter 1:15-16). The call is not to a technique. It is to resemble God, "without which no man shall see the Lord" (Hebrews 12:14). A church that is genuinely waiting for Christ to return cannot hold its body in dishonor and love its brother carelessly and live as a parasite on its neighbors, because the One it waits for is holy, and the waiting makes you ache to be found like Him when He comes. We stop searching for the hidden will of God the moment we obey the plain one.

God called you to be holy.

## Grief With a Floor Under It
*The dead in Christ, the descending Lord, and the children of the day*

**Text:** 1 Thessalonians 4:13-5:11 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 15:20 · John 11:25 · 2 Peter 3:10 · Romans 13:12

Someone in the Thessalonian church has died, and the survivors are coming apart. They believed Jesus was coming back soon, and now their friends are in the grave, and the terrible question hangs in the air: did the ones who died too soon miss it? Paul writes into raw grief, and he does not tell them to stop crying. He does something better. He puts a floor under the grief so it has somewhere to land.

**Not grief denied, grief with hope**

"I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Not that ye sorrow not. That ye sorrow not as others which have no hope. Paul never tells the Christian to stop grieving. He tells the Christian to grieve differently, with a hope underneath that the rest of the world does not have. He calls death sleep, not because death is gentle but because for the believer it is no longer final. You do not panic over a sleeper. You know he wakes.

And here is the ground the hope stands on: "If we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him" (1 Thessalonians 4:14). The whole argument rests on a historical fact. Jesus died and rose. Because the Head rose, the body must follow, "now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept" (1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstfruits means the rest of the harvest is coming. The empty tomb is not only His past. It is your future. Take away the resurrection and this comfort is sentiment, a kind thing said over a grave that changes nothing in it. Leave the resurrection where it belongs and the grave becomes a bed.

**The Lord Himself will descend**

Then Paul tells them exactly what happens, and it is not a metaphor. "The Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord" (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17).

The Lord himself. Not an angel sent in His place. Not a force. The same Jesus who stood at Lazarus's tomb and said, "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (John 11:25), comes down personally to collect His people, and He raises the dead ones first. So the very thing the Thessalonians feared, that their dead had been left behind, turns out backwards. The dead in Christ go first. Nobody is left out. Nobody arrived too late. And the last clause is the one to hold: so shall we ever be with the Lord. The hope of heaven is not a place. It is a Person, and never being apart from Him again. "Wherefore comfort one another with these words" (1 Thessalonians 4:18). These words. Not better feelings, not a softer way of saying goodbye. These specific promises spoken over a grave, that the Lord Himself is coming, that the dead rise first, that we will never again be separated from Him or from them.

**Children of the day, awake at their post**

Then Paul turns from the dead to the living, and the tone shifts. The day is coming, and it comes without warning. "The day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Peter saw the same thing: "the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise" (2 Peter 3:10). A thief does not send a calendar invitation. He comes when the house is asleep.

So Paul draws the line between two kinds of people. "Ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day: we are not of the night, nor of darkness. Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober" (1 Thessalonians 5:5-6). The world is asleep, drugged on its own security, saying "Peace and safety" right up to the moment "sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape" (1 Thessalonians 5:3). The church is to be awake. Not anxious, awake. Sober. Dressed for the day. "Putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation" (1 Thessalonians 5:8), which is the same charge Paul gave Rome: "the night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light" (Romans 13:12).

Now let it cut where it should. I confess I live more like the sleeping world than the watching church. I say peace and safety with my schedule. I build as though the day will never interrupt me, and I let the hope of His coming become a doctrine I affirm instead of a reality I order my life around. I have nodded at the trumpet and the descending Lord on a Sunday and then planned my Monday as though none of it were true. The Thessalonians were grieving toward that day. Most of us are simply distracted from it.

But hear the floor Paul lays under all of it, the reason the children of the day can sleep at night and wake for the morning without terror: "God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, that, whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him" (1 Thessalonians 5:9-10). Whether we wake or sleep. Whether you are alive when He comes or already in the grave, the verdict is the same: together with Him. The thief comes for the world. For you He comes as a Bridegroom. That is the difference the cross makes, the Lord who died for us has already absorbed the wrath that the day brings on the world, so the very day the unprepared dread is the day His own people have been longing for. It is the only thing that lets a Christian stand at a graveside and weep without despair. "Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do" (1 Thessalonians 5:11).

Grieve, but not without hope.

## The Faithful God Will Keep You
*Final commands for a church learning how to wait*

**Text:** 1 Thessalonians 5:12-28 · **Supporting:** Philippians 4:6-7 · Ephesians 4:30 · Jude 24 · 1 Corinthians 1:8-9

Paul ends the way he began, pointing them to the day Christ returns, but now he fills the waiting with commands. They come fast, almost without breath, a dozen of them stacked one on another, and it would be easy to hear them as a checklist. They are not. They are the shape of a life that is genuinely waiting for the Lord. A church that believes He is coming back lives a certain way, and Paul is sketching it.

**The life of a waiting church**

First, toward leaders and toward each other: "know them which labour among you... esteem them very highly in love for their work's sake. And be at peace among yourselves" (1 Thessalonians 5:12-13). Then the harder work of a real congregation: "warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men. See that none render evil for evil" (1 Thessalonians 5:14-15). Notice he does not flatten people into one category. The unruly need a warning. The fainthearted need comfort. The weak need holding up. Mature love does not treat everyone the same way; it gives each person what that person actually needs, and it costs you to know the difference. It is far easier to have one posture for everyone, all severity, or all softness, than to learn a person well enough to know which one they need today. The waiting church does the harder thing.

Then come the three commands the church has turned into a wall hanging and stopped obeying: "Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you" (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18). We read those and feel scolded, because we cannot imagine doing them under pressure. But remember who is reading them first, a persecuted church burying its dead. Paul is not asking for a cheerful mood. He is describing a life so anchored to the returning Christ that joy and prayer and thanks keep running even when everything else is on fire. This is Philippians made portable: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts" (Philippians 4:6-7). The thanks is not denial of the hard thing. It is defiance of it. You give thanks in the affliction precisely because the affliction is not the last word and you know who has the last word.

Then toward God's work among them: "Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Abstain from all appearance of evil" (1 Thessalonians 5:19-22). Do not put out the fire God is lighting, "grieve not the holy Spirit of God" (Ephesians 4:30), but do not be gullible either. Test everything. Keep the good. Walk away from the evil. A waiting church is neither cynical nor naive. It is discerning. The cynic quenches the Spirit to feel safe. The gullible swallows everything to feel spiritual. Paul forbids both and asks for the harder, slower work of weighing each thing and keeping what is true.

**The command we cannot obey, and the One who can**

And here is where the whole thing would crush us, because nobody keeps this list. Read it honestly and you fail it by the third line. Rejoice always, I do not. Pray without ceasing, I do not. Give thanks in everything, I do not, not in the hard things, not when I am afraid. If the church's standing depended on the church's performance of this list, every one of us would already be lost. I have preached this very chapter and then gone home and worried, and prayed about almost nothing, and given thanks for less.

Paul knows it. So watch what he does the instant he finishes the commands. He turns from what we must do to what God will do. "And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Thessalonians 5:23). And then the line that holds the entire letter up: "Faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it" (1 Thessalonians 5:24).

Who also will do it. Read the commands again in that light and they change from a burden into a promise. The God who calls you to be blameless is the God who will make you blameless. Your perseverance is not finally your achievement; it is His faithfulness. Paul said it to Corinth the same way: God "shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful" (1 Corinthians 1:8-9). The day is coming, and you will be found standing on it, not because you white-knuckled a list, but because the One who started this in you is faithful and "is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy" (Jude 24).

Now let it land where it should. We are exhausted because we have been trying to keep ourselves. We treat the Christian life as a performance we sustain by effort, and then we wonder why we are tired and afraid of the coming day instead of longing for it. Paul lifts the weight off. He gives the commands, they are real, and the waiting church obeys them, and then he hands the outcome to God. You are not the one keeping you. The faithful God is keeping you, and He will not lose you, and He will not fail to finish what He began before His Son splits the sky.

So you can rejoice. So you can pray. So you can give thanks in the fire and bury your dead in hope and warn the unruly and hold up the weak and wait, awake and unafraid, for the One who is coming. Not because you are strong. Because He is faithful, and He will do it.

The faithful God will keep you.
